groups.title: At the faculty registration desk

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Good morning. Engineering registration desk. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Hi. I'm a second-year student, and I'm trying to add an elective, but the online system keeps saying I don't meet the prerequisite.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Which course is it?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Introduction to Urban Design. It's offered by the Faculty of Architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I see. Most of their courses require Basic Drawing first. Have you taken that?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Not here, but I did a drawing course at a summer program last year. I have a certificate.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: In that case, you can apply for a prerequisite waiver. You'll need two signatures: one from the course instructor and one from your own academic advisor.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Two signatures? My advisor, Dr. Siriporn, is away at a conference until Thursday. And the add-drop period ends on Friday, doesn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Yes, at four o'clock. But if you hand in the waiver form before then, we'll hold a seat for you, even if the signatures come in later.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: That's a relief. Where can I get the form?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: It's on the faculty website under Student Forms, or I can print one for you right now.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: A printed copy would be great, thanks. Oh, and is there a fee for adding a course this late?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Not until the second week of term. You're still in the first week, so it's free.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Perfect. Then I'll email Dr. Siriporn right away and try to see the course instructor this afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: You look worried. What's up?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: I just got an email from the library. Apparently I owe six hundred baht in fines.

dialogue.speaker: Woman

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Very funny. It's only three books, but one of them was a reserve item, and those are charged by the hour, not by the day.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Oh no. I made exactly the same mistake in my first year. Reserve books are only supposed to leave the building for two hours.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: I know that now. The worst part is that I can't register for next semester until the fine is paid. The system just blocks you.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Have you thought about appealing? The library has a form for that.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: An appeal? On what grounds? It was my own fault.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Not necessarily. Maybe the reserve label was missing, or maybe you were ill. They do reduce fines sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Actually, now that you mention it, the label was half torn off. I honestly thought it was a normal loan.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: There you go. Take a photo of it before you return the book, and attach it to the appeal.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Good thinking. But if they turn me down, I'll still have to pay before registration opens on the fifteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: At least you'll have tried. And next time, set a reminder on your phone the moment you check something out.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Believe me, I've learned my lesson.

groups.title: Biology lecture: bees and pollination
groups.text:
Good morning, everyone. Last week we looked at how some plants rely on the wind to carry their pollen. Today we're turning to a far more precise method, one that most flowering plants depend on: pollination by animals, and in particular, by bees.

Let's start with a simple question. Why does a bee visit a flower at all? It isn't to help the plant, at least not on purpose. Bees are after food. Nectar gives them energy, and pollen gives them protein to feed their young. As a bee moves around inside a flower, pollen grains stick to the fine hairs that cover its body. When it lands on the next flower of the same kind, some of those grains rub off, and the plant can be fertilised.

Now, here's the interesting part. Many bees show what biologists call flower constancy. On a single trip, a bee tends to visit only one type of flower, even when other types are blooming right next to it. From the plant's point of view, that's extremely valuable, because pollen delivered to the wrong species is simply wasted.

Plants, in turn, have developed ways of attracting bees. Bees can't see red very well, but they can see ultraviolet light, which we can't. Many flowers that look plain to us actually carry ultraviolet patterns that guide bees toward the nectar, rather like the landing lights on an airport runway.

Finally, a word about why all this matters outside the textbook. Around the farming town of Ban Rai Dok, growers of a local melon variety saw their harvests fall by almost a third over five years. When researchers from Northvale Agricultural College studied the fields, they found far fewer wild bees than before, mainly because the hedges where the bees nested had been cleared to make room for more crops.

For next week, please read chapter eight, and think about what those farmers might do differently.

items.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How farmers can grow larger melons
Why bees are unable to see red
How bees help flowering plants reproduce
Why wind pollination is more effective

groups.title: Campus radio: exam-week update
groups.text:
Good afternoon, and welcome to Campus Update on Radio Kanchana, the student station of Kanchana University. With final exams starting next Monday, here's what you need to know about services on campus over the next two weeks.

First, the main library will be open twenty-four hours a day throughout the exam period. Between midnight and six in the morning, however, only the ground floor and the second floor will be available, and after ten p.m. you'll need to show your student ID card at the entrance, so please don't leave it in your room.

Group study rooms can be booked online as usual, but there's a limit of three hours per group per day. And here's an important change: if your group hasn't checked in within fifteen minutes of the start of your booking, the room will be released to the next group on the waiting list.

Next, transport. The free shuttle bus between the library and the dormitories will run much later than usual, right through until one o'clock in the morning. If you're planning a late night, check the timetable on the university app before you set off.

The main cafeteria will close at nine p.m. as usual, but the student union is setting up a snack corner on the library's ground floor, with free drinking water, fruit and sandwiches from eight until midnight.

Finally, a reminder from the examinations office: bags are not allowed in any exam hall. Lockers are available in the lobby of Building Four, so arrive a little early to leave your things there.

That's all from Campus Update. Good luck with your exams, and remember: a few hours of sleep may do more for your grades than one more hour with your notes.

To explain the rules of a student radio contest

groups.title: A short history of tea
groups.text:
Tea is now so ordinary that it is easy to forget how unusual it once was. According to an old legend, the drink was ___1___ by accident when leaves from a wild bush blew into a pot of boiling water. Whether or not the story is true, historians agree that tea was first drunk in southwestern China, ___2___ early drinkers often boiled the leaves with salt, ginger or even onions. The light, clear drink that most people know today developed only ___3___, over many centuries.

For a long time, tea was traded in the form of hard bricks made of pressed leaves. These bricks were easy to carry and did not spoil quickly; ___4___, in some remote regions they were used as money. Merchants carried them on horseback along narrow mountain routes, a journey that ___5___ several months.

Tea reached Europe in the early seventeenth century. At first it was so expensive that only wealthy families could ___6___ it, and some households kept their supply in locked wooden boxes. ___7___ prices fell, tea spread from grand houses to ordinary kitchens. In Britain, the custom of a light afternoon meal with tea and small cakes became a social habit ___8___ survives in some form even now.

The worldwide demand for tea also had less pleasant ___9___. Large plantations were established in several countries, and the workers on them often laboured long hours for very low pay. Historians today stress that the story of tea is not only one of taste and tradition, ___10___ also one of trade, power and human cost.

groups.title: The surprising story of the pencil
groups.text:
The ordinary pencil is so cheap and familiar that few people stop to think about how it is made. Yet its history is surprisingly ___1___. In the sixteenth century, shepherds in northern England noticed a soft black material in the ground that left dark marks ___2___ rubbed against stone. At first, they used it to mark their sheep. People believed the substance was a type of lead, and this mistaken idea explains ___3___ we still speak of pencil "lead" today, even though pencils have never contained any.

The material was in fact graphite, a form of carbon. Because pure graphite is soft and breaks easily, early users wrapped sticks of it in string or sheepskin. ___4___, someone had the idea of placing the graphite inside a hollow wooden holder, which kept the user's fingers clean and made the tool much stronger.

A major problem remained: good graphite was ___5___, and the best deposits were controlled by a small number of owners. In the late eighteenth century, a French engineer found a way to ___6___ this shortage. He mixed powdered graphite with clay and baked the mixture in an oven. By changing the amount of clay, he could make the pencil harder or softer, an idea that ___7___ the basis of the grading system still printed on pencils.

Mass production in the nineteenth century made pencils available to almost everyone. Factories ___8___ thousands of them every day, and schools began to use them instead of slates. Today, even in an age of screens and keyboards, billions of pencils are sold each year, ___9___ they are reliable, need no power and can be erased. It seems that this simple tool, ___10___ humble origins lie in a field of sheep, is not ready to disappear.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถาม
groups.title: Why teenagers struggle to wake up
groups.text:
For generations, parents have complained that teenagers stay up too late and refuse to get out of bed in the morning. The usual explanation has been a moral one: young people are lazy, or they waste the evening on their phones. Research over the past few decades, however, suggests that the picture is more complicated. Part of the problem lies not in teenagers' habits but in their biology.

Every human being has an internal clock, a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours that tells the body when to feel alert and when to feel sleepy. One of the signals that controls this cycle is melatonin, a hormone released in the evening as daylight fades. In young children, melatonin rises early, which is why many of them are ready for bed soon after dinner. During adolescence, however, the release of melatonin shifts later, often by one to two hours. A fifteen-year-old who lies down at nine o'clock may simply stare at the ceiling, not because she is being difficult but because her body has not yet received the signal to sleep.

This shift would matter less if school timetables followed it. In many places, though, secondary schools start earlier than primary schools, partly because of bus schedules and the working hours of parents. The result is a mismatch: students are asked to concentrate at the very time their internal clocks tell them they should still be asleep. Teachers often notice the effect in the first lesson of the day, when classes are noticeably quieter and slower.

Some school districts have experimented with later start times. In a three-year study of eleven secondary schools in the Westbrook Valley district, researchers from Calderwood University compared students before and after the morning bell was moved from 7:30 to 8:30. On average, students slept about forty minutes more per night, and attendance in first-period classes rose by six percent. Interestingly, students did not simply go to bed later to make up for the change; their bedtimes stayed roughly the same.

Critics point out that later starts are not free. Bus routes have to be redesigned, after-school sports may finish in the dark, and parents who need to be at work early may find it harder to arrange care for younger children. These are real concerns, and the Calderwood researchers themselves admit that a change that works in one district will not necessarily suit another.

Even so, the research has changed the conversation. Instead of asking only how to make teenagers more disciplined, educators are beginning to ask how schools might work with adolescent biology rather than against it. For the teenager who struggles to wake up, that change in thinking may be the most welcome news of all.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถาม
groups.title: Streets for people
groups.text:
For most of the twentieth century, city planners asked one main question when they designed a street: how many cars can it carry? Wide roads, large intersections and generous parking were seen as signs of progress. Pedestrians were expected to fit into whatever space remained, often a narrow pavement squeezed between traffic and buildings.

In recent decades, a growing number of planners have begun to question this approach. Their argument is simple. A street is not only a channel for movement; it is also a public space where people meet, shop, rest and play. When a street is designed only for cars, it tends to become a place that people pass through as quickly as possible rather than a place where they wish to stay.

The coastal city of Port Selwyn offers a useful example. Ten years ago, its old market district was dominated by a four-lane road that cut the neighbourhood in two. Shop owners complained that customers rarely stopped, and the noise made outdoor seating impossible. After long public consultations, the city narrowed the road to two lanes, widened the pavements, planted rows of shade trees and added protected lanes for bicycles. Several side streets were closed to through traffic altogether.

The changes were controversial at first. Some drivers predicted endless traffic jams, and a few businesses feared that customers who arrived by car would stop coming. Neither prediction fully came true. Traffic on the main road did slow down, but much of it moved to a ring road built for that purpose, and journey times across the city rose only slightly. Meanwhile, a survey by the Port Selwyn Chamber of Commerce found that the number of people walking through the district at weekends nearly doubled within three years, and two-thirds of local shops reported higher sales.

Planners warn against treating such results as a universal recipe. Port Selwyn had advantages that not every city shares: a compact centre, a mild climate and a ring road that could absorb the displaced traffic. In a sprawling city where homes, schools and workplaces are far apart, simply removing lanes might create congestion without persuading anyone to walk.

What the example does show is that the shape of a street influences how people behave on it. Wide, fast roads invite fast driving; narrow, shaded streets with places to sit invite people to slow down. The question for planners, then, is no longer only how many cars a street can carry, but what kind of life they want it to support.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถาม
groups.title: The ocean's slow conveyor
groups.text:
Seen from a beach, the ocean can look like a vast, still body of water that merely rises and falls with the tides. In reality, it is constantly on the move. Enormous currents carry water across entire ocean basins, transporting heat, nutrients and even floating objects thousands of kilometres from where they started.

Surface currents are driven mainly by the wind. As steady winds blow across the sea, they drag the top layer of water along with them. Because the Earth is rotating, these currents do not travel in straight lines; they are turned to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. The result is a series of huge circular patterns, known as gyres, that turn slowly in each of the major oceans.

Deep currents work quite differently. They are driven not by wind but by differences in the density of seawater, which depends on its temperature and how much salt it contains. Cold, salty water is heavier than warm, fresher water. In parts of the far North Atlantic, surface water becomes so cold and salty in winter that it sinks to the ocean floor and begins to creep southward. Warmer water flows in at the surface to replace it. Scientists sometimes call this system the global conveyor belt, because it links all the world's oceans in one continuous loop. A single body of water may take a thousand years or more to complete the journey.

These movements have a powerful effect on climate. Warm currents carry heat from the tropics towards the poles, which helps to explain why some coastal regions are far milder than others at the same distance from the equator. Currents also bring nutrients up from the deep, supporting rich fishing grounds in places where cold water rises to the surface.

Oceanographers have used some unusual methods to trace these paths. When the cargo ship Meridian Star lost a container of plastic bath sponges in a storm in the North Pacific, a team led by researcher Halvard Eng began collecting reports of sponges washing ashore. Over the next six years, sponges turned up on beaches in four countries, and the pattern of where and when they appeared helped confirm computer models of the gyre. Today, scientists rely mostly on networks of floating instruments that send data by satellite, but accidental experiments of this kind still attract public interest.

Some researchers are concerned that a warming climate could weaken the deep circulation. They point out that if melting ice adds large amounts of fresh water to the North Atlantic, the surface water there may no longer become heavy enough to sink. Exactly how quickly such a change could happen is still debated, but most scientists agree that the ocean's slow conveyor matters far more to life on land than its calm surface suggests.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถาม
groups.title: Before and after the printing press
groups.text:
When people think of the invention of printing, they often picture a single moment: a workshop in fifteenth-century Germany and a press turning out the first printed books in Europe. The real story is longer and far more widely spread. Printing developed over many centuries, and several of its most important steps took place in Asia.

The earliest widely used method was woodblock printing. A craftsman carved an entire page of text, in reverse, into a flat block of wood. Ink was spread over the raised surface, paper was laid on top, and the back of the paper was rubbed to transfer the image. The technique was well established in China by the ninth century. Woodblocks had an obvious drawback, however: each block could print only one page, and a single mistake might ruin days of careful carving.

The solution was movable type, in which each character was made as a separate piece that could be arranged, used and then rearranged for the next page. Records describe an eleventh-century Chinese craftsman who made individual characters out of baked clay. Later printers experimented with wood and, in Korea, with metal. Yet movable type did not quickly replace woodblocks in East Asia. Written Chinese uses thousands of different characters, so a printer needed an enormous stock of type and a well-organised system for finding each piece. For many books, carving whole blocks remained the more practical choice.

In Europe, conditions were different. Alphabetic writing needed only a few dozen letters, plus numbers and punctuation marks, which made movable type far more economical. When metal type was combined with an oil-based ink and a screw press adapted from those used for squeezing olives, printing spread with remarkable speed, and within a few decades presses were operating in hundreds of towns.

The effects went far beyond the workshop. Books became cheaper, so more people could own them, and identical copies made it easier for scholars in different cities to discuss the same text. The historian Ingrid Vasel argues that this sameness was as important as the lower price: "For the first time, a reader in one city could point to page forty and know that a colleague hundreds of kilometres away was looking at exactly the same words." Mistakes could be corrected in later editions instead of multiplying with every handwritten copy.

None of this means that one region "won" the history of printing. Rather, the technology developed differently in different places because it had to fit different writing systems, materials and markets. Seen this way, the story of printing is less about a single inventor than about how people in many places adapted a powerful idea to their own needs.

groups.title: Why we buy the medium size
groups.text:
Most shoppers like to think that they make decisions by carefully comparing price and quality. Consumer psychologists, however, have shown again and again that our choices are strongly shaped by the way options are presented. Two of the best-known examples are anchoring and the decoy effect.

Anchoring describes our tendency to rely heavily on the first number we see. Imagine a jacket displayed with a label reading "Was 4,000 baht, now 2,400 baht." The original price acts as an anchor; compared with it, 2,400 baht feels like a bargain, even if the jacket was never really worth 4,000. Shoppers who see the same jacket labelled simply "2,400 baht" typically judge it as less attractive, although the price is identical.

The decoy effect is more subtle. It occurs when a seller adds an option that few people are expected to choose, simply to make another option look better. In an experiment at a cinema, researchers from Lindqvist Business School offered customers small popcorn for 60 baht and large popcorn for 110 baht. Most people chose the small size. When the researchers added a medium size for 100 baht, sales of the large size rose sharply. The medium option was not really meant to be bought; it existed to make the large one seem like excellent value for only ten baht more. Indeed, very few customers chose it.

Retailers use these techniques for an obvious reason: they work. Restaurants place one very expensive dish at the top of a menu so that everything below it looks reasonable. Online stores display a "premium" subscription that almost nobody needs, which makes the "standard" plan look sensible. None of these methods involves lying, and many shoppers would be surprised to learn that they had been influenced at all.

Does this mean consumers are helpless? Not necessarily. Researchers suggest a few simple habits. Before shopping, decide roughly how much you are willing to spend, so that your own figure, rather than the seller's, becomes the anchor. When you are faced with several options, ask whether you would still choose the same item if the most expensive or the cheapest option were removed. And be especially careful with phrases such as "only ten baht more," which turn attention away from the total price and towards a small difference.

Understanding these effects is not about becoming suspicious of every price tag. It is about recognising that the human mind takes shortcuts, and that sellers know this as well as psychologists do. A shopper who understands the shortcuts is in a far better position to decide when to take them.

items.stem: The number of tea plantations [[increased]] rapidly, [[and]] working conditions on [[it]] were often [[harsh]].
items.explanationTh: คำที่ถูกแทนคือ plantations ซึ่งเป็นพหูพจน์ จึงต้องใช้ "them" ไม่ใช่ it

items.stem: Urban trees [[provide]] shade, [[reduce]] noise, and [[making]] streets [[more pleasant]] for pedestrians.
items.explanationTh: กริยาสามตัวที่ขนานกัน (provide, reduce, make) ต้องอยู่ในรูปเดียวกัน จึงต้องเป็น "make"

items.stem: [[Unlike]] wind-pollinated plants, [[which]] produce huge amounts of pollen, [[insect-pollinated]] plants [[needs]] far less.
items.explanationTh: ประธาน insect-pollinated plants เป็นพหูพจน์ กริยาจึงต้องเป็น "need"
